extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers, conference organizers (Area Chairs/PCs), reviewers, and developers/researchers building AI tools for peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for writing and assessing conference peer reviews (ICLR-style) and for evaluating AI-assisted review tools (e.g., automated report cards, rating predictors). Includes review-form criteria, scoring scales, and metrics for judging AI outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions. This is not the place to critique the paper; the authors should generally agree with a well-written summary. This is also not the place to paste the abstract — please provide the summary in your own understanding after reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise restatement of contributions in your own words that demonstrates understanding of the submission. Avoid copying the abstract verbatim; the summary should reflect that you read the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the paper. A good mental framing for strengths and weaknesses is to think of reasons you might accept or reject the paper. Please touch on the following dimensions: Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain concrete reasons supporting acceptance or rejection; relate points to the Quality/Clarity/Significance/Originality dimensions. Use this section to motivate subsequent numerical ratings and to give actionable signals for authors/ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported (e.g., by theoretical analysis or experimental results)? Are the methods used appropriate? Is this a complete piece of work or work in progress? Are the authors careful and honest about evaluating both the strengths and weaknesses of their work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate Quality on a 1–4 scale (4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor). Base the rating on technical correctness, thoroughness of evaluation, appropriateness of methodology, and honesty/rigor in presenting results and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written? Is it well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? Note that a superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate Clarity on a 1–4 scale (4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor). If unclear, give constructive suggestions for organization, exposition, and what additional details (e.g., proofs, experimental settings) are needed for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results impactful for the community? Are other researchers or practitioners likely to use the ideas or build on them? Do the results provide difficult-to-obtain conclusions about existing data or unique theoretical or experimental approaches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate Significance on a 1–4 scale (4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor). Discuss who would be affected by the results and whether the contribution advances the field meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work provide new insights, deepen understanding, or highlight a task in a better way than previous work? Does it introduce novel contributions, unique data, or demonstrate improved properties (efficiency, fairness, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate Originality on a 1–4 scale (4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor). Originality need not be a wholly new method; novel combinations, evaluations, or insights can be rated highly — justify the rating by comparing to prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric component ratings (Quality/Clarity/Significance/Originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on what you discussed in Strengths and Weaknesses please assign the paper a numerical rating on the following scale to indicate each dimension: 4 excellent, 3 good, 2 fair, 1 poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 4-point scales consistently for each named dimension and ensure the written strengths/weaknesses support the numeric choices. These numeric ratings feed downstream decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions and Actionable Suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Please list and carefully describe questions and suggestions for the authors which should focus on key points — ideally around 3–5 that are actionable with clear guidance. Think of things where a response from the author can change your opinion, clarify a confusion, or address a limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clear criteria under which your evaluation score could increase or decrease. Make questions and suggestions specific and actionable (e.g., what experiment/data/analysis would change your view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and Negative Societal Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors adequately addressed the limitations and potential negative societal impact of their work? If so simply leave yes; if not please include constructive suggestions for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be rewarded for being upfront about limitations. Provide concrete, constructive recommendations for how limitations or societal concerns could be mitigated or better discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (1–10) with descriptive rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall score for this submission on a 1–10 scale where each numeric value has a descriptive meaning (10 Strong Accept ... down to 1 Desk Reject). Examples: 10 = Strong Accept: Technically flawless paper with groundbreaking impact; 5 = Reject; 1 = Desk Reject: major violations or out-of-scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided 10-point descriptors to map qualitative judgments into the overall numeric score. Describe why the paper falls at that point on the scale, referencing the earlier dimension-specific analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a confidence score for your assessment to indicate how confident you are in your evaluation. Choices: 5 = absolutely certain (very familiar, checked math/other details) down to 1 = educated guess (not in your area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a confidence level honestly and use it to qualify your recommendations (e.g., low confidence should make ACs weigh your review accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage (review content coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review address key aspects like novelty, significance, technical soundness, empirical validation, related work depth, presentation, and ethical considerations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out any missing topics (e.g., omitted empirical validation or ethics). For automated feedback, surface overlooked dimensions and explicitly mention what was omitted and why it matters (e.g., link missing score changes to rebuttal arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity (concreteness/actionability of critiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the critiques concrete and actionable? Did the reviewer provide page/line references, concrete rewrites, or surgical suggestions rather than high-level comments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage line-level edits, figure-specific suggestions, explicit experimental recommendations, or exemplary mini-case studies. Prefer requests that enable a response that could change the reviewer’s assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence base (substantiation of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review substantiate its claims with quotations, equations, empirical numbers, citations, or concrete examples from the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should provide evidence for assertions (e.g., quoting theorem statements, pointing to equations/figures, referencing empirical numbers). Avoid unsubstantiated assertions like 'significant practical implications' without rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the feedback framed to help authors improve? Does the review suggest revisions or experiments that would make the submission stronger?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructive suggestions over dismissive commentary. Provide actionable guidance (e.g., which datasets/benchmarks, what ablations, how to rewrite a paragraph) and reward reviewers who suggest clear paths to improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the language professional, respectful, and collegial? Does the review avoid dismissiveness and encourage revision where appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain politeness and a constructive frame. Note minor language issues but avoid ad hominem or dismissive phrasing. Tone is part of review quality and can be flagged by automated tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted composite scoring of review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate multiple review-dimensions (e.g., Coverage, Specificity, Evidence Base, Constructiveness & Tone) into a weighted composite score using specified weights (example weights: 0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.25 producing a 1–5 composite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the per-dimension scores and weights transparently. Use composite scores to standardize feedback quality signals for ACs or to nudge reviewers toward evidence-based critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer report-card dimensions (Coverage/Specificity/Constructiveness/Tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate a 'Reviewer Report Card' that explicitly rates a human review along Coverage, Specificity, Constructiveness, and Tone, with summaries and suggested improvements per dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use few-shot examples to train/generate these cards; evaluation is qualitative and should be judged by experienced reviewers or ACs for Accuracy, Helpfulness, and Actionability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for LLM-generated review components (Accuracy / Helpfulness / Actionability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating AI-generated review content (e.g., strengths/weaknesses or report cards), assess: Accuracy (does the AI correctly identify strengths/weaknesses?), Helpfulness (would the feedback help the reviewer improve?), and Actionability (are the suggestions concrete?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is primarily qualitative using expert raters; sample metrics include proportion of AI points judged valid (precision) and proportion of human points captured (recall). Experts should rate usefulness and whether suggestions are implementable.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-Judge semantic coverage (precision & recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a powerful LLM as a 'judge' to compare human review points and AI-generated points: list distinct human (real) points and count how many generated points overlap. Compute precision (fraction of AI points that are valid) and recall (fraction of human points captured by AI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt the judge with checklist format: Real points: <number> - [<point1>, ...]; Hits (overlap): <number>. Use the resulting counts to compute precision/recall as quantitative proxies of semantic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating-prediction evaluation (final-score prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given paper text, an initial review and author rebuttal, predict the final score after considering the rebuttal. Evaluation may focus on exact score, direction of change (increase/decrease/no change), and magnitude (e.g., +/-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicting exact final scores is hard; direction and magnitude may be more informative. This task requires datasets where reviewers explicitly state why their score changed; otherwise models learn from coarse signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompting and few-shot structure for review-component generation
rubrics_metrics.description: When using ICL/few-shot prompting to generate review components, provide examples showing paper title/abstract/content, potential strengths/weaknesses, initial score/review, and author rebuttal where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize prompts to mirror the review task (EXAMPLE 1, EXAMPLE 2, ACTUAL TASK). Include REVIEW_GUIDELINES at the top to keep outputs aligned with conference expectations; include explicit instructions for the LLM-as-Judge evaluation step where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and data-collection safeguards (for AI-assisted review systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-assisted review systems should preserve privacy, mitigate bias and misuse, have clear institutional policies on AI use and author declarations, and rely on ethically-sourced, structured deliberation data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect fine-grained deliberation data only with robust privacy safeguards and minimal user burden. Design for continuous ethical auditing (bias detection, fairness metrics) and transparent pilot programs with community engagement.
